QUINCY (1838-1848)

UNDER the shadow of Boston State House, turning its back on the house of John Hancock, the little passage called Hancock Avenue ran from Beacon Street to Mount Vernon Street on the summit of Beacon Hill; and there, in the third house below Mount Vernon Place, February 16, 1838, a child was born and christened later by his uncle, minister of the First Church after the tenets of Boston Unitarianism, as Henry Brooks Adams. Had he been born in Jerusalem under the shadow of the Temple and circumcised in the Synagogue by his uncle the high priest, under the name of Israel Cohen, he would scarcely have been more distinctly branded, and not much more heavily handicapped in the races of the coming century. Yet a traveller ticketed through life by an old, established traffic found safeguards as convenient as they were irksome. Whether life was an honest game of chance, or whether the cards were marked and forced, he could not refuse to play his excellent hand. To his life as a whole he was a consenting, contracting party and partner from the moment he was born to the moment he died.

As it happened, he never got to the point of playing the game at all; he lost himself in the study of it, watching the errors of the players; but this is the only interest in the story, which otherwise has no moral and little incident. A story of education—seventy years of it—the practical value remains to the end in doubt; although every one cannot be a Gargantua-Napoleon-Bismarck and walk off with the great bells of Notre Dame, every one must bear his own universe, and most persons are moderately interested in learning how their neighbors have managed to carry theirs.

For him alone the old universe was thrown into the ash-heap and a new one created. He and his eighteenth-century, troglodytic Boston were suddenly cut apart—separated forever—by the opening of the Boston and Albany Railroad; the appearance of the first Cunard steamers in the bay; and the telegraphic messages which carried from Baltimore to Washington the news that Henry Clay and James K. Polk were nominated for the Presidency. This was in May, 1844; he was six years old; his new world was ready for use.

Of the preparation, he knew only the color of yellow. He first found himself sitting on a yellow kitchen floor in strong sunlight. The second lesson was taste: on December 3, 1841, he developed scarlet fever, and though he remembered not the faintest detail of illness, he remembered his aunt entering with a saucer and a baked apple. The third was discomfort: bundled in blankets, carried from Hancock Avenue to Mount Vernon Street on January 10, 1842, he never forgot the want of air and the noise of moving furniture.

The fever, seeming trivial to the child, took greater importance to the man. He fell behind his brothers in height and bone; his mind shared the fining-down of scale. He was not good in a fight; his nerves were more delicate than boys’ nerves ought to be. The habit of doubt; of distrusting his own judgment and of totally rejecting the judgment of the world; the tendency to regard every question as open; the hesitation to act except as a choice of evils; the shirking of responsibility; the love of line, form, quality; the horror of ennui; the passion for companionship and the antipathy to society—none peculiar to New England character—seemed in him to have been stimulated. His brothers were the type; he was the variation.

The atmosphere of education was colonial, revolutionary, almost Cromwellian. Resistance to something was the law of New England nature; hatred of evil was a duty, and boys learned betimes that politics, as a practice, whatever its professions, had always been the systematic organization of hatreds. The charm of New England was harshness of contrasts and extremes of sensibility—a cold that froze the blood, and a heat that boiled it—so that the pleasure of hating—one’s self if no better victim offered—was not its rarest amusement. Winter and summer, town and country, force and freedom, marked two modes of life and thought, balanced like lobes of the brain. Town was restraint, law, unity; country was liberty, diversity, outlawry, the endless delight of mere sense impressions given by nature for nothing.

Boys are wild animals, rich in the treasures of sense, and the New England boy had a wider range than boys of equable climates. To the boy Henry Adams, summer was drunken. Smell was strongest—hot pine-woods and sweet-fern; new-mown hay; ploughed earth; box hedges; peaches, lilacs, syringas; stables and cow-yards; salt water and low tide on the marshes; nothing came amiss. Next to smell came taste, and the children knew the taste of everything from pennyroyal and flagroot to the shell of a pignut and the letters of a spelling-book—the taste of A-B, AB, suddenly revived on the boy’s tongue sixty years afterwards. Light, line, and color came later. The New England light was glare; color, a peony with morning dew; the intense blue of the sea from the Quincy hills; June cumuli; the strong reds and greens and purples of children’s picture-books. The opposites were the cold grays of November and the thick, muddy thaws of Boston winter. After a January blizzard, the boy who could look with pleasure into the violent snow-glare scarcely knew what was meant by tone. He could reach it only by education.

Winter and summer were two hostile lives. Winter was always the effort to live; summer was tropical license. Whether rolling in the grass, wading in the brook, swimming in the salt ocean, sailing in the bay, fishing for smelts, netting minnows, chasing muskrats, hunting snapping-turtles, or gathering mushrooms and nuts, summer and country were always sensual living, while winter was always compulsory learning. Summer was the multiplicity of nature; winter was school. The bearing of the two seasons on the education of Henry Adams was no fancy; it was the most decisive force he ever knew, and made the division between irreconcilable problems, irreducible opposites, with growing emphasis to the last year of study.

Quincy, two hours’ walk from Beacon Hill, belonged to a different world. For two hundred years the Adamses had lived within sight of State Street, yet none took kindly to the town, or was taken kindly by it. Never for a moment did the boy connect the two ideas of Boston and John Adams; they were separate and antagonistic; the idea of John Adams went with Quincy. Boston had bathrooms, a water-supply, a furnace, gas; Quincy had none of these comforts and no Boston style. The old house at Quincy was eighteenth century; what style it had was in Queen Anne mahogany panels and Louis Seize chairs brought back from Paris; neither comfortable. With childish prejudice he never quite overcame, he cared little for nineteenth-century plush and fashions; he was born an eighteenth-century child.

Between boy and master there was always war. A boy’s will is his life, and he dies when it is broken. Yet his first serious contact with the President—his grandfather—left no sting. One summer morning he rebelled against going to school. At the foot of the library stairs, the old man opened the door, put on his hat, took the boy’s hand, and without a word walked with him, paralyzed by awe, up the shadeless road to town. The boy planned to dodge; the old man never stopped; he seated the culprit in school, released his hand, and departed. He had shown no temper; above all, he had held his tongue. No revolting cant about duty and obedience passed his lips. For this intelligent silence the boy felt instinctive respect.

During those summers the President admitted him to a sort of familiarity that must have tried patience. He hung about the library; deranged papers; ransacked drawers; drew the sword-cane; snapped the travelling-pistols; penetrated the dressing-closet where tumblers, inverted on a shelf, covered caterpillars that were to be butterflies, but never were. The Madam protested when her best cut-glass bowls were planted with acorns to watch roots grow, and left like the caterpillars to be forgotten. The President rode the hobby of tree-culture; peaches and pears, the best of their kind, came up to rot for seed. With Puritan virtue, the boy brought him the finest peaches and ate only the less perfect. Somewhere there still exists a little volume of critically edited Nursery Rhymes, with the boy’s name in full written in the President’s trembling hand on the fly-leaf. Of course there was also the Bible, given to each child at birth, with the proper inscription; while their grandfather Brooks supplied the silver mugs.

A cottage was built “on the hill,” with a far view over Quincy Bay and Boston. Till his twelfth year he passed summers there. The sharpest home impressions were of kindred, and none warped a mind more than the back of the President’s bald head in his pew on Sundays, in line with that of President Quincy, while over it the boy read the tablet to a President great-grandfather who had “pledged his life, his fortune, and his sacred honor.” The Irish gardener once said: “You’ll be thinkin’ you’ll be President too!” The casual remark so fixed itself that the boy never forgot it; he had never thought on the subject; that there should be a doubt was a new idea.

The Madam was more remote, more decorative, and to the boy an exotic. He liked her refined figure; her gentle voice; her panelled room with Dutch tiles; her Sevres and Queen Anne mahogany; her writing-desk with little glass doors and little eighteenth-century volumes labelled Peregrine Pickle, Tom Jones, Hannah More. She could never be Bostonian, which was her cross and her charm. Born in London in 1775, daughter of Joshua Johnson of Maryland and Catherine Nuth, she had been carried to Nantes, then back to London, where President Washington made her father Consul. In 1797 John Quincy Adams married her in London and took her to Berlin; in 1801 they came to America; in 1809 to St. Petersburg, where she lost a little girl and, in the winter of 1814-15, alone with a boy of seven, crossed Europe in her travelling-carriage during the Cent Jours. Then came London again; in 1817 Washington as Secretary of State’s wife; next four miserable years in the White House; afterwards fifteen years more as the wife of a Member of the House. By 1843-48, when the boy remembered her at breakfast with heavy silver teapot and sugar-bowl and cream-jug, she was seventy and weary of a stormy world; a vision of silver gray, hardly more Bostonian than on her wedding-day.

From her, though he did not know it, he might inherit those doubts and rebellions which marked more than one descendant; he was not pure New England stock, but half exotic. Even as a child of Quincy he had a quarter taint of Maryland blood. Charles Francis, half Marylander by birth, had hardly seen Boston till he was ten; he was nearly as old as his mother before Boston accepted him, or he accepted Boston.

This prehistoric stage ended abruptly. One winter morning in Mount Vernon Street the word paralysis attached itself to the President, and thenceforward the boy saw him in a tall-backed armchair beside the spare-bedroom fire. The end came February 21, 1848. If the scene on the floor of the House, when the old President fell, struck Americans with a sensation unusually dramatic, the funeral service in the Quincy church, conducted by Dr. Lunt—refined, dignified, with deeply cadenced voice and remarkable English—left an overwhelming impression on the boy’s mind. Later, in Faneuil Hall, he heard his uncle Edward Everett’s Eulogy, admirable oratory too good for a ten-year-old, yet already the boy knew that the dead President could not be in it, and why. The shadow of the War of 1812 still hung over State Street; the shadow of the Civil War to come had begun to darken Faneuil Hall. How could Mr. Everett whisper Hartford Convention before the men who had made it? What would have been said had he suggested Secession?

At ten years old he stood face to face with a dilemma: What was he?—where was he going? Something was wrong; it must be Boston. Quincy represented a moral principle—the principle of resistance to Boston. Turn the dilemma as he pleased, he came back on the eighteenth century and the law of Resistance; of Truth; of Duty, and of Freedom. He was a ten-year-old priest and politician. Supposing he had seen a New York stock-list of 1900, and studied the statistics of railways, telegraphs, coal, and steel—would he have quitted his eighteenth-century prejudices and ideals, and gone down to State Street to ask for the fatted calf of his grandfather Brooks and a clerkship in the Suffolk Bank? Sixty years afterwards he was still unable to make up his mind. Each course had its advantages, but the material advantages, looking back, seemed to lie wholly in State Street.
